subtopics.title: Hydrogen train specifications
subtopics.summary: India's first indigenous Hydrogen-powered Train was inaugurated by PM Modi on the Jind–Sonipat route in Haryana. It is configured as a 10-coach Hydrogen Fuel Cell Trainset powered by a 1,200 kW propulsion system. The train was developed by Integral Coach Factory, Chennai, and its approved operational speed is 75 km/h against a design speed of 110 km/h. Hydrogen is the lightest chemical element, and it makes up nearly 75% of the universe's normal matter.

Propulsion: 1,200 kW Hydrogen Fuel Cell Propulsion System
Approved operational speed: 75 km/h; design speed: 110 km/h

subtopics.title: Components of the hydrogen train
subtopics.summary: The hydrogen train combines fuel cells, batteries, a hydrogen storage system and traction motors. Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells generate electricity from hydrogen and oxygen. Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries store surplus electricity, while high-pressure cylinders hold the compressed hydrogen needed for propulsion. Electric traction motors convert electrical energy into mechanical energy to drive the train.
facts: Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells generate electricity through an electrochemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen
Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries store surplus electricity generated by fuel cells
Hydrogen Storage System: high-pressure cylinders store compressed hydrogen required for propulsion
Electric Traction Motors convert electrical energy into mechanical energy to drive the train
Four major components: fuel cells, LFP batteries, hydrogen storage, traction motors

subtopics.title: Indian Railways: history and network
subtopics.summary: Railways were introduced in India in 1853, between Bombay and Thane, during the tenure of Governor General Lord Dalhousie. India ranks fourth globally in railway infrastructure, and the network has 19 zones. Tracks are classified as Broad, Metre or Narrow gauge, with Broad Gauge measuring 1.676 m. The Konkan Railway, constructed in 1998, runs 760 km from Roha to Mangalore.

subtopics.title: New developments in railways and S&T
subtopics.summary: KAVACH is an indigenous Automatic Train Protection System developed by RDSO, with automatic braking and centralised live monitoring. The Vande Metro train has been renamed Namo Bharat Rapid Rail, and Namo Bharat/RapidX runs on the Delhi–Ghaziabad–Meerut corridor. Mission 41K aims to save Rs 41000 crore over 10 years through energy-efficient solutions. The Amrit Bharat Station Scheme plans to redevelop 400 major stations by tying up with private companies.

quizzes.title: How the hydrogen train works
quizzes.passage: India has inaugurated its first indigenously built hydrogen-powered train, which will run on a route connecting Jind and Sonipat in Haryana. The train is configured as a trainset of several coaches, and its power comes from a fuel cell propulsion system. Each part of the train has a separate role, and the train works only when these parts function together. Inside the train, fuel cells generate electricity through a reaction between hydrogen and oxygen. This electricity is not always used at once, so the surplus is stored in batteries for later use. The hydrogen itself is carried in cylinders that keep the gas compressed until the propulsion system needs it. Electric traction motors then convert electrical energy into mechanical energy, and this mechanical energy drives the train forward. The train's approved operating speed is set below its design speed, so it is allowed to run more slowly than it is built to run. Hydrogen is the lightest chemical element and is the most abundant element in the normal matter of the universe. Indian Railways has also introduced other technologies in recent years, including the KAVACH safety system and the Namo Bharat Rapid Rail. In short, the fuel cells are the source of power, the batteries store surplus power, the cylinders store the fuel, and the motors drive the train.

quizzes.title: Indian Railways: facts and figures
quizzes.passage: Railways came to India in the mid nineteenth century, when the first line was opened between two cities in western India during the tenure of a Governor General. The network is now organised into administrative zones, and its tracks are of different widths. The country classifies these tracks into three groups based on the distance between the rails. Each zone manages a part of the national network. Some lines run through hilly terrain, and a few of them are known as mountain railways. In recent years, the government has focused on upgrading stations, raising speeds and adding safety systems. New high-speed trains have been introduced on several routes, including services with names such as Tejas and Humsafar. One long project links Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka, and it passes through difficult terrain. A financial arm supports the investment that such projects need. Several new schemes also aim at redeveloping stations and cutting energy use, which shows that the network is being modernised in many areas at once. Passenger services and station projects all depend on the same network, so planning must cover many needs at once. Track width is one of the ways the network's lines are described and compared. Several of these changes were announced in the same period, which shows the scale of the planned upgrades.
